Better nom Error Messages with nom_locate

August 2026

Parsing Parser Errors

I'm extracting NeoDoc's parser from my static site generator. It's built using a Rust parser/combinator crate called "nom". It's fantastic. Except for the part where the error messages are cryptic as hell. For example, this code uses nom's alt feature to try three different ways to parse an input string:

[package]
name = "default_errors"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
nom = "8.0.0"
use nom::branch::alt;
use nom::bytes::complete::tag;
use nom::{IResult, Parser};

fn main() {
  let input = "prelude target";
  let result = starter(input);
  std::fs::write(
    "output.txt",
    format!("{:#?}", result),
  )
  .unwrap();
}

fn starter(input: &str) -> IResult<&str, &str> {
  let (input, _) = tag("prelude").parse(input)?;
  let (input, result) =
    alt((alfa, bravo, charlie)).parse(input)?;
  Ok((input, result))
}

fn alfa(input: &str) -> IResult<&str, &str> {
  let (input, result) = tag("xxx").parse(input)?;
  Ok((input, result))
}

fn bravo(input: &str) -> IResult<&str, &str> {
  let (input, result) = tag("yyy").parse(input)?;
  Ok((input, result))
}

fn charlie(input: &str) -> IResult<&str, &str> {
  let (input, result) = tag("zzz").parse(input)?;
  Ok((input, result))
}

All three parsers fail since the "target" portion of the input string doesn't match any of their patterns (i.e. "xxx", "yyy", and "zzz"). nom throws an error when parsing fails. Here's what it looks like for this example:

Err(
    Error(
        Error {
            input: " target",
            code: Tag,
        },
    ),
)

  • The input: " target" shows us that the "prelude" portion of the string got slurped up properly and only the target remains.

  • The code: Tag lets us know that the error was generated because on of the attempts to use a .tag() failed.

    Critically, it doesn't tell us which one of the three failed.

Figuring out the issue in this example is no big deal. It's quick to see that neither of the alfa, bravo, or charlie parsers match the target string that was passed to them. Things are rarely so straight forward to spot in more complicated parsers. Each of the branches could call multiple child parers that call ones further down the tree, etc.

It doesn't take long to cross a threshold where figuring out where an error occurred is a non-trivial task.

I used to use another crate called "nom_supreme" on top of nom. It provided errors with more details about where they came from. The problem is that nom had a major version upgrade a while back. nom_supreme doesn't work with the new iteration.

That's where nom_locate enters the scene.

Locating Errors

nom_locate works by adding a LocatedSpan struct to the mix. Your &str input gets passed around inside it.

Cargo.toml 
[package]
name = "locate_basic"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
nom = "8.0.0"
nom_locate = "5.0.0"
use nom::bytes::complete::tag;
use nom::{IResult, Parser};
use nom_locate::LocatedSpan;

type Span<'a> = LocatedSpan<&'a str, &'a str>;

fn main() {
  let input = "target";
  let span = Span::new_extra(input, "");
  let result = parser(span);
  std::fs::write(
    "output.txt",
    format!("{:#?}", result),
  )
  .unwrap();
}

fn parser(mut span: Span) -> IResult<Span, Span> {
  span.extra = "parser";
  let (span, result) =
    tag("prelude").parse(span)?;
  Ok((span, result))
}
Err(
    Error(
        Error {
            input: LocatedSpan {
                offset: 0,
                line: 1,
                fragment: "target",
                extra: "parser",
            },
            code: Tag,
        },
    ),
)

-- endnote
